newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak central bank move seen ending forex play.
newsitem.headline: Slovak central bank move seen ending forex play.

text.p: New Slovak central bank measures due to be phased in from the end of this year will probably force commercial banks to stop -- and reverse -- a lucrative investment play, bankers say.

Local bankers expect the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) to announce later this month details of the measures, part of a package announced in mid-July which was aimed at reining in a rapidly growing money supply and curbing short-term lending.
Many domestic banks, faced with a lack of medium and longer-term funds on the crown market, have repatriated foreign exchange assets and converted them into crowns.
The crowns are then deposited at other local banks to take advantage of Slovak interest rates, which are seven to 10 percentage points higher than on foreign currencies.
In some cases, banks have taken out foreign currency loans to fund the same investment, bankers say.
But the NBS unveiled its package of measures on July 16 due to worries that high money supply growth would push up Slovak inflation, one of the lowest in post-communist Europe.
The key money supply measure, M2, grew 21 percent year-on-year in July.
The measures were also aimed against short-term lending which does little to help the Slovak economy to modernise.

They included widening the band in which the Slovak crown is fixed daily against a dollar/mark basket to introduce more foreign exchange risk, raising the requirement for banks' minimum reserves and increasing the NBS's Lombard rate.
A further technical measure appears to be aimed at discouraging the foreign currency play.

From December 31, banks must exclude foreign exchange assets held locally from their foreign exchange position for monetary purposes. They will also have to include crown liabilities to banks outside Slovakia.
This effectively increases their liabilities and limits foreign exchange assets against local banks and their clients.
Banks must also reach a minimum ratio of foreign exchange assets and liabilities of 0.65 by December 31, rising to at least 0.7 from March 31, 1997 and at least 0.8 by June 30.

Some banks already meet the ratio requirements. But the NBS moves -- especially the different calculations of assets and liabilities -- are likely to force many to move in the opposite direction, increasing their assets abroad by converting crowns into foreign exchange and depositing them outside Slovakia.
"This will bite," said a foreign analyst, who requested anonymity. "This will make banks reverse what they have been doing until now."

"The ratio can only be met once banks transfer (foreign exchange) assets in loans to residents into loans to non-residents, or increase their nostro accounts, meaning exactly the opposite development," said Silvia Majlingova, a head of the Liquidity Department at CSOB Bank Bratislava.
Nostro accounts are those held by Slovak banks abroad.

Slovak capital account figures for the first half of 1996 indicated a drop in the banks' assets abroad, recording a surplus of $434.3 million in June on the short-term financial account, after a $281.1 million deficit in the end of 1995.
"Banks will have to meet the ratio by the end of 1996, and it will be a big problem, as banks have their commitments ...," Majlingova added.
-- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-210-3687
